# Education in Nigeria
Education in Nigeria is structured into primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, governed by policies aimed at universal access and quality. Primary education starts around age five, lasting six years, with subjects including Mathematics, English, religious knowledge, sciences, and indigenous languages. The Universal Basic Education (UBE) program, established in 1999, mandates nine years of free and compulsory schooling covering both primary and junior secondary education, overseen by the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC).
Secondary education follows a 6-3-3-4 or revised 9-3-4 system, with three years each for junior and senior secondary divisions. Core subjects are supplemented by electives including sciences, arts, and vocational studies. Federal government also sponsors “unity schools” known for merit-based admissions. Teacher qualifications vary by school type, with private schools generally having better-qualified teachers and facilities compared to often understaffed state schools. Secondary education culminates in national exams conducted by the West African Examination Council (WAEC) and National Examination Council (NECO). Private and religious schools charge high tuition but offer smaller class sizes and often higher educational standards.
Tertiary education includes public and private universities, polytechnics, and colleges, with over 150 universities registered. Admission primarily depends on secondary school exam results and the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) exam. Universities offer multi-year programs varying by discipline. Vocational education is overseen by the National Board for Technical Education and includes formal certifications alongside widespread informal apprenticeships. Despite reforms, challenges persist including teacher shortages, unequal resource distribution, literacy gaps (especially in northern regions), and accessibility issues, particularly for girls and rural populations. Initiatives by government and NGOs aim to reduce gender disparities, improve teacher training, and increase literacy rates, with an ongoing focus on expanding digital literacy towards a 95% national target by 2030.
